vignette:
He was fifty years old, a clinical psychologist with a private practice, a man who had spent two decades guiding others through their darkest hours. He came to see me after a referral from a colleague, his voice steady but his hands restless, gripping the armrest of the chair as if it might disappear.

The event happened three years ago, on a Thursday evening in late autumn. He had been at a professional conference, a routine gathering of peers. After a late dinner with colleagues, he walked back to his hotel alone through a poorly lit parking lot. A man appeared from behind a van, pressed a knife to his ribs, and forced him into a service alley. The assault was methodical, silent, and brief. He remembers the cold concrete against his back, the smell of asphalt and stale cigarette smoke, the way the man's face remained half-hidden in shadow. He remembers thinking, I know how to handle this. I know the protocol. Stay calm, don't provoke, survive. He did survive. When it was over, he walked back to his hotel, showered, sat on the edge of the bed, and did not call anyone.

He told no one for six weeks. Not his wife, not his partners at the practice. He continued seeing clients, listening to their trauma narratives with an unnerving composure that he now recognizes as dissociation. In session, he would sometimes feel his own pulse in his throat, but he forced himself to focus. He thought he could compartmentalize. He had taught others how to.

But the symptoms crept in like ivy through a cracked wall. He began avoiding the parking lot of the conference hotel, then any hotel parking lot at dusk. He took longer routes home to avoid alleys. He stopped attending evening professional events altogether, citing vague "personal reasons." He started having panic attacks during supervision sessions when a supervisee described a client's sexual assault. He would excuse himself to the restroom, lock the stall, and press his fists against his eyes until the spinning stopped.

Sleep became a battleground. He lies awake for hours, replaying the alley, the knife, the silence. When he does sleep, he dreams of being pinned down, unable to scream. He wakes with his jaw clenched so tight his teeth ache. His wife has stopped reaching for him in bed. He knows she senses the distance, but he cannot explain. Every time he tries, the words turn to dust in his mouth.

He started procrastinating case notes. He began to dread certain clients-those who reminded him of the attacker's build, or those who were angry, or those who cried. He felt a shame rooted deep in his chest, a whisper that he should have fought, should have seen it coming. He, of all people, knew the statistics. He knew that knowledge does not immunize. But knowing and feeling are two different rivers.

At work, he has become cautious to the point of rigidity. He double-checks the locks on his office door between sessions. He has asked the receptionist to screen all walk-ins. He avoids the storage closet by the fire exit because it reminds him of the alley's darkness. His colleagues notice his fatigue, his evasiveness, but he deflects with self-deprecating jokes about being "overdue for a vacation."

Last week, during a session with a male client who disclosed a childhood sexual assault by a stranger, he felt a surge of rage so sudden and hot that he had to grip the arm of his chair. His voice remained calm, professional-he asked the client to describe a safe place-but inside, he was back in that alley, the knife cold, his heart a trapped bird. After the session, he sat in his office with the lights off for twenty minutes.

He has not been able to tell any of this to his wife. He has not been able to tell his own therapist, because he does not have one. He is a psychologist. He knows the model. He has watched his own mind turn against him. He tells me, with a hollow laugh, that he is his own worst case study. Then he falls silent.

He stares at the floor for a long time. His PCL-5 score is 53. I do not tell him that. He knows, and he knows what it means. He just does not yet know how to let himself be the one who is helped.
